question: How much faster is S3 Express One Zone than S3 Standard, and is it cheaper per request?
reference_answer: S3 Express One Zone offers data access speeds up to 10x faster than S3 Standard, with request costs 50 percent lower than S3 Standard.
evidence: with data access speeds up to 10x faster and with request costs 50 percent lower than S3 Standard

question: What kinds of S3 buckets are there, and how many directory buckets and table buckets can I create by default?
reference_answer: S3 has four bucket types: general purpose, directory, table, and vector buckets. By default you can create up to 100 directory buckets per AWS account, and up to 10 table buckets per account per Region (with up to 10,000 tables per table bucket).
evidence: Amazon S3 supports four types of buckets—general purpose buckets, directory buckets, table buckets, and vector buckets.
notes: Bucket types are listed on p31, the directory bucket limit on p32, and the table bucket limit on p33.

question: Is there a size limit on a bucket policy?
reference_answer: Yes. Bucket policies are limited to 20 KB in size.
evidence: Bucket policies are limited to 20 KB in size.

question: If I overwrite an object and read it right away, do I get the new data? And if I delete a bucket and immediately list my buckets, will it be gone?
reference_answer: Yes for objects: S3 gives strong read-after-write consistency for PUT and DELETE requests on objects, so a read after a successful overwrite returns the new data. Bucket configurations are only eventually consistent, so a deleted bucket might still show up in an immediate bucket listing (and AWS recommends waiting 15 minutes after first enabling versioning before writing).
evidence: If you delete a bucket and immediately list all buckets, the deleted bucket might still appear in the list.
notes: Object consistency is on p37 (also summarized on p30); the bucket-configuration eventual consistency is on p38.

question: Can new customers still start using S3 Object Lambda?
reference_answer: No. As of November 7, 2025, S3 Object Lambda is available only to existing customers already using it and to select AWS Partner Network (APN) partners. Alternatives include Dynamic Image Transformation for Amazon CloudFront, invoking AWS Lambda by other means, or processing data in the client application.
evidence: S3 Object Lambda as of November 7th, 2025 is available only to existing customers that are currently using the service
notes: p29 still describes S3 Object Lambda as a feature without the availability caveat, so a retriever that returns only p29 would produce a misleading answer.

question: I just made a new AWS account. What should I do so I'm not using the root user for everyday work?
reference_answer: First secure the root user: sign in to the console as the root user and turn on multi-factor authentication (MFA). Then enable IAM Identity Center, grant administrative access to a user there, and sign in as that user with the sign-in URL sent to your email.
evidence: Turn on multi-factor authentication (MFA) for your root user.
notes: The root-user sign-in step starts on p46; MFA, IAM Identity Center, and admin user steps are on p47.

question: When I create a bucket in the console by copying settings from an existing bucket, does the bucket policy get copied too? Can I do the same from the CLI?
reference_answer: No. The copy-settings option does not copy the bucket policy from the existing bucket, and it is only available in the Amazon S3 console, not in the AWS CLI.
evidence: Doesn't copy the bucket policy from the existing bucket to the new bucket
notes: The same console create-bucket procedure appears twice (Getting started p49 and Creating a general purpose bucket p122). Either page fully answers the question.

question: I want to turn on Object Lock while creating a bucket in the console. What permissions do I need, and does it change versioning?
reference_answer: Enabling Object Lock automatically enables versioning for the bucket, and after creation you must also configure the default retention and legal hold settings on the bucket's Properties tab. To create an Object Lock enabled bucket you need s3:CreateBucket, s3:PutBucketVersioning, and s3:PutBucketObjectLockConfiguration.
evidence: Enabling Object Lock automatically enables versioning for the bucket.
notes: The versioning fact is on p53 and the permissions note on p54. The same permissions note also appears in the CLI walkthrough on p70 (and p69 says Object Lock requires versioning), so [69, 70] is an acceptable alternative retrieval.

question: How do I download an older version of a file from my bucket in the S3 console?
reference_answer: Open the S3 console, choose General purpose buckets (or Directory buckets), and choose the bucket. Turn on Show versions next to the search box, select the check box next to the version you want, and choose Download (or Actions > Download as to save it to a specific folder).
evidence: If you want to download a specific version of the object, turn on Show versions (located next to the search box).
notes: Steps 1-3 are on p55; the Show versions step is on p56.

question: How do I delete a bucket in the console when it still has files in it?
reference_answer: First empty it: select the bucket, choose Empty, type 'permanently delete' to confirm, and choose Empty. Then select the bucket, choose Delete, type the bucket name to confirm, and choose Delete bucket. Neither action can be undone, and after deletion another account can take the bucket name.
evidence: To confirm that you want to empty the bucket and delete all the objects in it, in Empty bucket, type permanently delete.
notes: Emptying is on p58; deleting the bucket is on p59.

question: How do I create a bucket in us-west-2 using the AWS CLI?
reference_answer: Use s3api create-bucket with a location constraint, because Regions other than us-east-1 require one: aws s3api create-bucket --bucket <name> --region us-west-2 --create-bucket-configuration LocationConstraint=us-west-2.

question: If I create a bucket with the AWS CLI and set SSE-KMS default encryption, are S3 Bucket Keys turned on automatically like they are in the console?
reference_answer: No. In the AWS CLI, S3 Bucket Keys are not enabled by default when creating a new bucket, unlike the console. You enable them by setting "BucketKeyEnabled": true in the put-bucket-encryption configuration.
evidence: In the AWS CLI, Amazon S3 Bucket Keys are NOT enabled by default when creating a new bucket.
notes: p53 states the console default (enabled) separately, but p71 states the contrast on its own.

question: How can I download only the .txt files from a bucket in one go with the CLI?
reference_answer: Use a recursive copy with exclude and include filters: aws s3 cp s3://<bucket>/ . --recursive --exclude "*" --include "*.txt".
evidence: aws s3 cp s3://amzn-s3-demo-bucket/ . --recursive --exclude "*" --include "*.txt"
notes: p73 notes that the CLI (unlike the console) can download multiple objects using wildcards or --recursive, so p73 is a reasonable extra hit.

question: Can I host a static website on S3 while keeping all Block Public Access settings turned on?
reference_answer: Yes. AWS recommends keeping Block Public Access enabled and serving the site through Amazon CloudFront with origin access control (OAC). CloudFront also adds security such as HTTPS, which S3 static website endpoints lack because they support only HTTP.
evidence: If you want to keep all four Block Public Access settings enabled and host a static website, you can use Amazon CloudFront
notes: p83 has the full explanation; p106 repeats the OAC recommendation briefly.

question: Can I create buckets in my account regional namespace in every AWS Region?
reference_answer: No. Account regional namespace buckets can be created in all AWS Regions except Middle East (Bahrain) and Middle East (UAE).
evidence: You can create buckets in your account regional namespace in all AWS Regions except Middle East (Bahrain) and Middle East (UAE).

question: How do I make sure people in my organization can only create buckets in our account regional namespace?
reference_answer: Use the s3:x-amz-bucket-namespace condition key in an IAM policy, Resource Control Policy, or Service Control Policy. The policy denies s3:CreateBucket when the condition StringNotEquals "s3:x-amz-bucket-namespace": "account-regional" is met, so only requests that set the x-amz-bucket-namespace header to account-regional succeed.
evidence: You can enforce that your IAM principals only create buckets in your account regional namespace. Use the s3:x-amz-bucket-namespace condition key.
notes: The IAM policy example is on p93. The RCP JSON and the SCP example continue on p94.

question: Should I put all my teams' data in one bucket separated by prefixes, or give each team its own bucket? What are the trade-offs?
reference_answer: A multi-tenant bucket with prefixes scales well for hundreds of datasets. However, bucket-level features such as default encryption, S3 Versioning, and Requester Pays can't be set per prefix, and cost allocation gets complex. A bucket per team or dataset lets you customize those settings and simplifies access management and cost allocation, but you may have to manage thousands of buckets (default quota 10,000, which can be raised), and AWS recommends creating them in your account regional namespace.
evidence: many S3 bucket-level features like default bucket encryption, S3 Versioning, and S3 Requester Pays are set at the bucket-level and not the prefix-level
notes: The multi-tenant pattern is on p96. The bucket-per-use pattern starts on p96, and its drawbacks and quota are on p97.

question: Why does an old bucket of ours in us-east-1 have uppercase letters and underscores in its name when I can't create one like that now?
reference_answer: Before March 1, 2018, buckets created in US East (N. Virginia) could have names up to 255 characters long that included uppercase letters and underscores. Since March 1, 2018, new buckets there must follow the same naming rules as all other Regions.
evidence: Before March 1, 2018, buckets created in the US East (N. Virginia) Region could have names that were up to 255 characters long

question: I'm using https://s3.amazonaws.com/<bucket> path-style URLs for a bucket in US West (Oregon) and getting an error. What error is it and why?
reference_answer: You get an HTTP 301 Permanent Redirect error. Except in US East (N. Virginia), path-style requests must use the Region-specific endpoint, and the error message indicates the correct URI for the resource.
evidence: if you use https://s3.amazonaws.com/bucket-name for a bucket that was created in the US West (Oregon) Region, you will receive an HTTP 301 Permanent Redirect error.

question: How do I serve files from my bucket under my own subdomain, like images.example.com?
reference_answer: Pick a hostname in a domain you control, create a bucket whose name exactly matches that hostname (e.g. images.example.com), and create a CNAME DNS record that aliases the hostname to the bucket's endpoint (e.g. images.example.com CNAME images.example.com.s3.us-west-2.amazonaws.com). Keep a matching bucket for every CNAME, and change or remove the CNAME if you delete the bucket.
evidence: Create a bucket that matches the hostname.
notes: Steps 1-2 and the dangling-CNAME warning are on p115; step 3 (CNAME record) is on p116. p114 also explains why the bucket name must equal the CNAME.
